passages.t: The golden statue and the command to bow
passages.happening:
King Nebuchadnezzar makes a golden statue sixty cubits high and six wide, and sets it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon (verse 1). He summons every official in the empire, satraps, prefects, governors, advisers, treasurers, judges and magistrates, to its dedication (verses 2-3).

A herald proclaims the command to ‘people of every nation and language’ (verse 4). As soon as they hear the music of horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp and pipes, they must fall down and worship the golden statue (verse 5). ‘And whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace’ (verse 6).

So when the music plays, the people of every nation and language fall down and worship (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 2 the king dreamed of a statue whose head of gold was himself, and he confessed Daniel's God as God of gods. Now he builds a statue of gold from head to foot, as if to say his kingdom will never give way to another. The confession of chapter 2 has not changed his heart.

The statue was about 90 feet high and 9 wide. Its narrow shape suggests a figure on a tall pedestal or a pillar, probably wood or another material overlaid with gold. Whether it stood for the king or his god is not said, though verse 12 links bowing to it with serving the king's gods. The plain of Dura was somewhere in the province of Babylon, and the exact site is unknown.

Public ceremonies of loyalty, where subjects bowed before a symbol of the king or his god, bound an empire's many peoples together. For most of the officials there, bowing was a civic formality that cost nothing, since many gods could be honored at once. For Jews bound by the first and second commandments, it was idolatry. What looks like politics to the empire is worship to the faithful.

The chapter repeats its lists again and again: the officials three times, the instruments four times, the golden statue and the blazing fiery furnace over and over. The pomp of the empire becomes almost comic. Three of the instrument names are Greek words, which those who date the book late take as a sign of the Greek period, and which those who date it early explain by Greek traders and craftsmen in the Near East before Alexander.
passages.later: The commandment the three men kept says, ‘You shall not bow down to them or worship them’ (Exodus 20:5). And Revelation warns against anyone who ‘worships the beast and its image’ (Revelation 14:9), in a book that draws constantly on Daniel's pictures.
passages.asks: The empire asked only for a moment of bowing when the music played. Ask what small public acts of loyalty your own world asks of you, and which of them would be worship. And ask how you would know the difference.

passages.t: Accused, and ‘But even if He does not’
passages.happening:
Some astrologers come forward and maliciously accuse the Jews (verse 8). They remind the king of his decree and name the three men he had set over the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who have ignored him and refused to serve his gods or worship the statue (verses 9-12).

Nebuchadnezzar, furious, summons them. Is it true? He gives them one more chance: when the music plays, bow, or be thrown into the furnace at once. ‘Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?’ (verse 15).

The three answer briefly. They have no need to defend themselves. ‘If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king’ (verse 17). ‘But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The accusation comes from rivals at court. The three men had been promoted at the end of chapter 2, and promotion brought enemies. The charge is framed as disloyalty to the king, but what is really at stake is worship.

The king's question in verse 15 is the question of the whole chapter. What god could deliver from the king's hands? He is sure of his answer. The chapter will answer it differently.

Against the noise of the empire's lists, the three men's reply is short and quiet. Verse 17 can be translated in two ways. Many versions read it as a confident statement that God is able and will deliver them. The BSB takes it as a condition, ‘If the God whom we serve exists’ (verse 17), meaning if he is as they believe. Either way, the climax is verse 18.

The first hearers were living under rulers who could demand what Nebuchadnezzar demanded. They were given a model of loyalty to the king in everything except worship, and of a faith that does not depend on being rescued.
passages.later: Isaiah had promised Israel, ‘When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched’ (Isaiah 43:2). And a psalm remembers, ‘we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance’ (Psalm 66:12).
passages.hard:
‘But even if He does not’ (verse 18). Does God always rescue the faithful?

The three men did not know they would be rescued, and they did not make their obedience depend on it. That is the heart of the chapter. In this story God does deliver them. But the book itself is honest that this does not always happen. In the visions, the wise ‘will fall by sword or flame’ (11:33), and the hope the book finally gives them is resurrection (12:2).

So this chapter is not a promise that faith will always be rewarded with escape. It is a picture of faith that would stand even without escape. No reader should take from it that someone who suffered or died for their faith, or for any other reason, lacked trust in God.

The chapter also records that astrologers ‘maliciously accused the Jews’ (verse 8). The story's sympathy is entirely with the accused. Nothing in it gives anyone a warrant for suspicion of the Jewish people, then or now.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The three men said even if he does not. Ask whether your faith depends on things turning out well. And ask where you are being asked to bow now, and whether you could say what they said.

passages.t: Into the fire, and a fourth man walking in it
passages.happening:
Nebuchadnezzar is filled with rage, and his face changes toward the three. He orders the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual, and commands strong men from his army to tie them up and throw them in (verses 19-20). They are thrown in bound, still wearing their robes, trousers and turbans (verse 21). The king's command is so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames kill the men who carried them up (verse 22).

Then the king jumps up in amazement. Did they not throw three men in, bound? He says he sees ‘four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire’ (verse 25), and that the fourth looks like a son of the gods.

He goes to the door of the furnace and calls them out as ‘servants of the Most High God’ (verse 26). They come out. All the officials gather and see that the fire had no power over them. ‘Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Execution by fire is known from the ancient Near East. Jeremiah mentions two men whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire. A furnace large enough to walk around in, with an opening above and a door at the side, fits the brick kilns that made Babylon's building materials.

The detail that the three were bound in all their clothes makes the rescue plainer. Their robes are untouched, and there is not even the smell of smoke on them. The fire that killed the soldiers outside did not harm the men inside.

The soldiers' deaths are told in a single verse. The story does not linger on them.

The king who asked what god could deliver from his hand is now the one who calls the three out by the name of the Most High God. The first hearers would have noticed who was bound and who was free: the men thrown in bound are walking loose, and the king is the one who runs to the door.
passages.later: Jeremiah records that the king of Babylon burned two men in the fire, and that the exiles used their names as a curse (Jeremiah 29:22). The letter to the Hebrews remembers people of faith who ‘quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword’ (Hebrews 11:34).
passages.hard:
Who was the fourth figure in the furnace?

The king says the fourth looks ‘like a son of the gods’ (verse 25), and a few verses later he says God ‘has sent His angel’ (verse 28). In the Aramaic, son of the gods is a pagan king's way of describing a divine being, not a title with a Christian meaning. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters therefore take the figure as an angel sent by God, as the king himself says. Many Christian interpreters, from the early church onward, have seen an appearance of the Son of God before his birth, connecting it with passages where the angel of the LORD speaks as God himself. The older King James rendering, like the Son of God, encouraged that reading.

The text itself leaves the figure as a divine messenger. These notes take no side. On every reading, the meaning is the same: God was present with his servants in the fire.
passages.asks: God did not keep the three out of the furnace. He met them in it. Ask where you have looked for God to keep you out of the fire, and whether you have looked for him in it. And ask what it would mean to come out of a hard thing with no smell of bitterness on you.

passages.happening:
Nebuchadnezzar declares, ‘Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him’ (verse 28). They defied the king's command and risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god but their own.

Then he decrees that anyone of any nation who speaks against their God will be cut into pieces and their houses turned to rubble, ‘For there is no other god who can deliver in this way’ (verse 29). And he promotes the three in the province of Babylon (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends as chapter 2 did, with a pagan king praising Israel's God and promoting the faithful. The question of verse 15, what god can deliver, has been answered by the king himself: no other god can deliver in this way. The verb for deliver, shezav, runs through the chapter to make the point.

The king's praise is real, but his habits have not changed. He still governs by threat. He has moved from threatening those who will not worship his statue to threatening those who speak against the God of the Jews. The book does not hold up his decree as a model. It shows a powerful man who has seen something true and still reaches for the furnace and the sword.

The word for serve, pelach, is used here for worship. The three would serve the king in government but would not serve his gods. The same word is used of the service all peoples give to the one like a son of man in chapter 7.
passages.later: The same pattern of a foreign king confessing Israel's God returns when Darius decrees that ‘men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel’ (Daniel 6:26), and when Nebuchadnezzar himself, humbled, praises the Most High (Daniel 4:34). A psalm sings of the same rescue: ‘The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them’ (Psalm 34:7).
passages.asks: The king saw a miracle and still governed by threats. Ask whether you have seen God act and still gone back to your old ways of controlling people. And ask how faith can be honored in a society without anyone being forced into it.
